rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Bodies in thermal contact exchange energy until **thermal equilibrium** — equal temperature, no net heat flow. The **zeroth law** states that if A and B are each separately in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other: equilibrium is transitive, and this transitivity is precisely what licenses thermometers to compare temperatures (NEB 2023, 2024).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - A ~ C and B ~ C ⇒ A ~ B - Equilibrium condition: T_A = T_B (no net heat flow)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Energy Conservation Foundation:** The first law ($\Delta U = Q - W$) is energy conservation applied to thermodynamic systems. Internal energy $U$ is a state function; heat $Q$ and work $W$ are path-dependent energy transfers. The sign convention: $Q > 0$ when heat enters the system, $W > 0$ when work is done BY the system.  ·  **Process Dependence:** $Q$ and $W$ depend on the thermodynamic path (isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric, isochoric), but $\Delta U$ depends only on initial and final states. For a cyclic process, $\Delta U = 0$ and $Q = W$ — net heat in equals net work out.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Some books define work on the system as positive and write ΔU=Q+Won; do not mix conventions.  ·  At constant volume, Q=ΔU only if no other work is present.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***NEB 2024*** — A~C, B~C ⇒ A~B: same temperature, no net flow on contact.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Equal temperature ≠ equal heat:** equilibrium equalises temperature, not energy content.  ·  **Zeroth, not third:** formulated after the first two laws but logically prior to them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: A gas absorbs 900 J and 350 J of work is done on it. Find ΔU using the stated convention.  ·  What does the first law imply for a complete cycle?

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Short (2m): Why does a thermometer need to stay in a liquid before reading?** — It must reach thermal equilibrium with the liquid (zeroth law); only then does its reading equal the liquid's temperature.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: The same 2m question appeared in 2023 and 2024 — a near-certain repeat.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **The thermometer's licence:** the zeroth law is what lets one instrument compare temperatures of many bodies.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: A~C and B~C ⇒ A~B (transitivity of thermal equilibrium).  ·  The zeroth law underlies the very definition of temperature.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Mercury-in-glass thermometers work only because glass+mercury reach equilibrium with the body measured.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Law That Makes Thermometers Possible Touch a hot stove and heat flows; touch a table and nothing happens. "Nothing happening" is thermal equilibrium — and the zeroth law turns it into a definition of temperature. Without it, comparing temperatures with a thermometer would have no logical basis.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2023, 2024) ### 2.1 Thermal equilibrium Two bodies in thermal contact are in **thermal equilibrium** when no net heat flows between them — they share the **same temperature**. Equilibrium is reached as energy transfers from the hotter to the colder body until temperatures equalise.…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 43:** equilibrium is the endpoint of heat flow. - **To Topic 45:** a mercury thermometer works *by* the zeroth law — it reaches equilibrium with the body and reports its shared temperature. - **To first law (Unit 11):** energy bookkeeping presupposes a well-defined temperature — supplied by the zeroth law.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Work in Thermodynamics:** Only $PV$-work is considered in the basic first law: $W = \int P_{ext} dV$. Reversible work uses the system pressure $W = \int P dV$. Other work forms (electrical, surface tension, magnetic) must be added as extra terms if present.  ·  Verified PYQs: zeroth law statement + numbering (2023, 2024 — 2m); A-C-B reasoning (2024 — 2m).  ·  "Bodies in thermal equilibrium have the same temperature."
